chapter_theme: Kannaki, standing over the fallen king and queen, names herself the heir of the chaste women of Pukar, swears that if she is a true pathini she will not let the kingdom or Madurai survive, tears off her left breast and flings it at the city, and the fire god, who says he long held an order to burn it on the day she was wronged, burns Madurai sparing only those she names; the closing venba says chastity ate the city and its gods withdrew.

cast.role: Kovalan's wife, who vows the destruction of Madurai and sets it burning
the Pandya's chief queen, fallen at his feet at the end of the last kaathai, addressed here as கோவேந்தன் தேவி
the Pandya king of Madurai who had Kovalan killed (named here as வழுதி, நற்றேரான்)
the fire god, who appears in a Brahmin's form (எரியங்கி வானவன்)
the women and men of Madurai, whom Kannaki calls to witness
the guardian gods of Madurai, who withdraw as the city burns

silappathikaram:21:1-16.reading: Kannaki tells the king's queen that she, a woman of cruel fate who knows nothing, still knows that he who harms another in the forenoon sees his own harm in the afternoon, and begins to list the chaste women of Pukar: one who made a vanni tree and a kitchen stand as witnesses, one who, told in play that a sand doll on the Ponni bank was her husband, would not leave it and was spared by the tide, and Karikal Valavan's daughter, who followed her Vanchi husband into the flood that took him until the sea brought him back to her.
silappathikaram:21:1-16.nuance: Kannaki calls herself கொடுவினை யாட்டியேன், a woman of harsh deeds or harsh fate, the same self-naming as the last kaathai's closing venba; she places herself under karma while, in the same breath, she threatens the king's house with the forenoon-afternoon law, so the deed's return is both a law and something she is about to carry out. The queen she addresses has just fallen at the king's feet, so the speech is made over the dead or dying. The exempla are told in clipped allusion and depend on stories the poem does not tell; who the sand-doll woman was and what the vanni tree witnessed are not given in these lines.
silappathikaram:21:1-16.event: Kannaki, addressing the Pandya queen, recalls the chaste women of Pukar one after another.

claims.claim: one who harms another in the forenoon sees his own harm come in the afternoon
a chaste wife's steadfastness can make a tree, a flood and the sea give way to her

silappathikaram:21:17-39.reading: Kannaki goes on with the women of Pukar, one who stood turned to stone until her husband came home, one who threw her own child into the well after her co-wife's child and brought both up, one who made her face a monkey's while her husband was away because another man stared, and the girl who, learning that her mother had promised her in play to a friend's son, put on new cloth and went with bowed head to him, then says that she was born in their city and, if she too is truly a pathini, will not let the kingdom live, will destroy Madurai, and the queen will see her vow kept.
silappathikaram:21:17-39.nuance: Lines 23 to 31 are nested speech: the girl's mother, telling the father, reproaches herself for not heeding the wise who say that a woman's wit is folly (பெண்ணறிவு என்பது பேதைமைத்தே) and for the careless word she spoke at the sand-house game; the saying is reported as a mother's self-blame, not asserted by the poem, and where the mother's speech begins is not certain. The vow is conditional on Kannaki's own virtue (பத்தினியே யாமாகில்), so the burning that follows is presented as the test that proves her a pathini, not only as revenge. The kaathai's name, வஞ்சின மாலை, takes the warrior's vow and gives it to a widow.
silappathikaram:21:17-39.event: Kannaki finishes her list of the chaste women of Pukar, vows to destroy the Pandya's kingdom and Madurai if she is a true pathini, and leaves the palace.

claims.claim: a true pathini's vow can end a kingdom and destroy its city

silappathikaram:21:40-57.reading: Kannaki calls the women and men of Madurai, the gods and the ascetics to hear that she, without fault, has raged against the royal city that wronged her beloved husband, twists off her left breast, circles Madurai three times and flings the breast into the street; the fire god appears as a Brahmin with red matted hair and white teeth and says he long held an order to feed this city to the fire on the day she was wronged and asks whom he should spare, and at her bidding to leave Brahmins, the virtuous, cows, chaste women, elders and children and go only to the side of the wicked, smoke and flame fill Koodal.
silappathikaram:21:40-57.nuance: Two causes stand side by side: Kannaki's own act and charge (சீறினேன் குற்றமிலேன் யான்) and the fire god's word that he had an order from long before (பண்டேயோர் ஏவ லுடையேன்), which makes the burning already decreed; who gave the order is not said. The fire takes a command from her (ஏவ, line 56), so a god serves the pathini's word. The exemptions limit her rage by a code of protected persons, and the city is burned as the king's, not as the guilty one's.
silappathikaram:21:40-57.event: Kannaki proclaims her grievance to Madurai, tears off her left breast and flings it at the city; the fire god appears, she names those to be spared, and Madurai burns.

claims.claim: a blameless wife whose husband was wronged by a king may rightly turn her anger on the king's city
the burning of the city on the day the pathini was wronged had been ordained beforehand
Brahmins, the virtuous, cows, chaste women, elders and children must be spared when a city is destroyed, and only the wicked struck

silappathikaram:21:58-61.reading: The closing venba says that the Pandya, his women, his palace, his army bright with bows and his horses and elephants were consumed as chastity ate fierce Koodal, and that the city's divine guardians vanished too.
silappathikaram:21:58-61.nuance: The venba names the agent of the burning as கற்பு itself, not Kannaki or the fire god. The sense of மாத்துவத் தான் (line 61) is not secure, so how the gods are said to vanish is uncertain.
silappathikaram:21:58-61.event: The fire consumes the Pandya's household, palace and army, and the guardian gods of Madurai withdraw.

claims.claim: chastity's power can consume a king with his house and army and drive a city's gods away

links.note: Kannaki states the forenoon-afternoon law of returning harm, in other words than the couplet's, as her warning to the Pandya's house.
links.teaches: The couplet's தாமே says the harm returns of itself with no agent, but the epic puts the law in the mouth of the woman who will herself bring the harm back that same day, so the impersonal return of a deed is shown working through a wronged person's act.

gains.a: her threat gains the standing of a known moral law rather than private revenge
gains.b: the couplet gains a case where the returning harm has a human executor and falls on a whole city, not only on the doer

links.note: Both tell of the husband of Karikal's line seized by the Kaveri flood at a festival; the akam poem leaves him taken, the epic has the sea bring him back to the wife who followed.
links.teaches: The Sangam memory of a lover lost to the river, which an akam courtesan uses as an image of a man taken away for good, is completed in the epic with a restoration won by the wife's steadfastness, turning a story of loss into an exemplum of chastity's power.

gains.a: the clipped allusion gains its back-story: the flood at Kazhar before Karikal in which the husband was seized
gains.b: the akam image gains a later ending in which the sea gives back what the river took, showing how the tale was retold as a chastity legend

links.note: Both are vanjinam vows in the conditional form 'if I do not, may I', one by a Pandya Nedunjeliyan before battle, one by Kannaki against a Pandya; the epic's king is not shown to be the Talaiyalanganattu victor of the puram poem.
links.teaches: The puram king stakes his own name as a just king on winning, while Kannaki stakes her name as a pathini on unmaking a king, so the epic turns the royal oath-form against the royal house and makes a widow's virtue the thing pledged.

gains.a: her vow gains the recognised form and force of the warrior's pledge, which explains the kaathai's name
gains.b: the puram oath-form gains a use outside war and kingship, showing that its penalty of being called a cruel king could be fulfilled by another's vow

links.note: Puram 9's Pandya warns cows, Brahmins, women, the sick and the sonless to take shelter before he attacks; Kannaki tells the fire to spare Brahmins, the virtuous, cows, chaste women, elders and children.
links.teaches: The protected classes of the just king's war reappear as the limit a wronged woman sets on her own vengeance against a Pandya city, so the code meant to restrain kings now restrains the one punishing a king, and is applied to his own capital.

gains.a: her list of the spared gains a precedent: it is the established rule of righteous attack, not a sudden mercy
gains.b: the poem's battle rule gains a case where it binds a non-king and is turned against the Pandya line whose ancestor proclaimed it

links.note: The couplet's wife commands the rain; Kannaki commands the fire god, who waits on her word.
links.teaches: Where the couplet's wife who worships no god has the rain at her word, the epic shows a god coming in person to take her orders, and the power that brings rain turned to burning a city, so the same claim for the chaste wife's word is shown in its most destructive extent.

gains.a: her command over the fire gains a known doctrine behind it: the chaste wife's word moves the elements
gains.b: the couplet gains a test case showing that the power it grants is not only beneficent and can set a god to destroy

links.note: Kannaki's dream of a harm to the city with the king, which she would not speak of, is fulfilled in the burning of the Pandya's house and Madurai.
links.teaches: The harm she refused to name in her dream turns out to be her own act, so the omen foretold not only the city's fall but the part the dreamer would play in it.

links.note: The patikam traces the ruin to a curse of a former birth ripening; the fire god here says he held an old order to burn the city, while Kannaki claims the act as her own rage.
links.teaches: Read together, the burning is caused three ways at once, by a karmic curse, by a standing divine order and by the wife's own deliberate act, and the epic does not choose between fate and her choice.

links.note: The venba's challenge to the queen to see what the woman of harsh deeds will do is made explicit as a vow to destroy the kingdom and Madurai.
links.teaches: The vague threat that closed the plea becomes a sworn vow with a condition on her own chastity, so the step from grievance to destruction is taken as an oath, not as a sudden fury.

new_concepts.gloss: the chaste wife whose steadfastness gives her word power over kings, cities and nature

source_issues: The kaathai header gives a printed last line of 55 against 61 lines held; the closing venba (58-61) and perhaps a difference of count in the akaval account for the gap.
Line 61 மாத்துவத் தான்மறைந்தார் has an unclear word (மாத்துவம்) and may be corrupt.
